text:
*Interview with Lina Ruedi, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Mademoiselle Ruedi, thank you for waiting. I will take the evening in order, one thing at a time. You were at dinner?

MLLE RUEDI: Yes, Monsieur.

MATTHEY: Tell me what happened when the temple struck nine.

MLLE RUEDI: The master made everyone show their watches, as he does every year. He told each owner what was wrong with theirs.

MATTHEY: And yours?

MLLE RUEDI: Mine was exact. I regulated it myself, and I know what it does.

MATTHEY: And the others?

MLLE RUEDI: Monsieur Félix's was twenty minutes behind. Monsieur Girard's was four minutes behind. The doctor's was two minutes ahead.

MATTHEY: Thank you. After dinner, where did you go?

MLLE RUEDI: Up to the atelier. I worked beside the master.

MATTHEY: Was the regulator on the wall there?

MLLE RUEDI: It was. When the temple struck ten, the regulator agreed with the bell exactly.

MATTHEY: What was the master doing?

MLLE RUEDI: Working at his bench, Monsieur. He was always particular about the regulator. He checked it against the bell as he checked everything.

MATTHEY: What happened after that?

MLLE RUEDI: He sent me downstairs when the regulator showed twenty past ten.

MATTHEY: Was the regulator running then?

MLLE RUEDI: Yes, Monsieur. It was running, and he was well.

MATTHEY: Did he say anything to you as you left?

MLLE RUEDI: Only what he always said, about the work I had left on the bench.

MATTHEY: Where did you go when you came down?

MLLE RUEDI: Straight down to the kitchen. I stayed there with Rosa from when I came down until after the temple struck eleven.

MATTHEY: Did you look at the time in the kitchen?

MLLE RUEDI: I compared my watch with Rosa's clock. Her clock was exactly fifteen minutes fast. She keeps it so on purpose, so that nothing is ever late.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything from the rest of the house?

MLLE RUEDI: Madame's piano. It began at twelve minutes to eleven by the kitchen clock, and it stopped at one minute past eleven by the kitchen clock.

MATTHEY: Do you know what Madame was playing?

MLLE RUEDI: Chopin, Monsieur. Madame plays Chopin better than anyone in this house.

MATTHEY: I should like to ask about the repeater. You worked on it with the master?

MLLE RUEDI: Some of it. He spent four years on that watch. He meant it to strike the first minute of the new century, and he was very exact about every part of it.

MATTHEY: Can you tell me how it speaks?

MLLE RUEDI: When you press the slide, the hours sound in low notes. Each quarter sounds as a doubled note. The minutes past the quarter sound in high notes. A person who knows the sound can tell the time from it in the dark.

MATTHEY: Is there anything about this evening you have not told me?

MLLE RUEDI: I have told you what I saw and heard, Monsieur. I have no opinions I would put to you.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Mademoiselle. Please wait in the hall. You may be asked to sign this when it is finished.
